name: Data Quality for AI
title: Data Quality for AI
answer: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. In practice this means the same checks a warehouse team already runs, applied to the tables that feed retrieval, training and reporting. The work sits close to the database, not in a separate quality tool, since the rows and the checks live in the same place.

sections.body: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. In practice this means the same checks a warehouse team already runs, applied to the tables that feed retrieval, training and reporting. The work sits close to the database, not in a separate quality tool, since the rows and the checks live in the same place.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is mostly the warehouse or database itself: SQL test suites, scheduled checks, constraint enforcement and versioned transformation code. Lineage is captured from query logs and orchestration metadata, and data contracts are stored as schemas or configuration alongside the pipelines they govern. On this site, 263 of the 2,650 tracked Model Context Protocol servers connect to SQL databases and warehouses, which is where a large share of these checks now run. Every page on this site is itself built from a PostgreSQL database, so the same discipline applies to the content you are reading.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams write assertions in SQL, for example row counts, null rates, uniqueness, referential integrity and range checks, then run them on a schedule or at pipeline boundaries. Failures route to an owner, and thresholds decide whether a run blocks or merely warns. Lineage maps which upstream tables feed which downstream models, so a broken column can be traced to everything it touches. Data contracts formalise the agreement between producers and consumers, covering schema, types, freshness and acceptable null rates.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership matters more than tooling: every critical table needs a named owner who answers for its quality. Contracts, lineage records and test results form the audit trail when a model produces a bad output and someone asks why. Access controls and retention rules apply to the quality metadata as well as the data, since lineage can reveal sensitive structure. Regulation and internal policy increasingly expect documented fitness for purpose, and quality evidence is how that is shown. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific obligations depend on the jurisdiction and the data involved.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect quality checks to move closer to the model, with contracts enforced at the point of retrieval rather than only at load. Agent and tool based access, including the SQL oriented Model Context Protocol servers tracked on this site, makes freshness and provenance checks part of the request path. Automated profiling and anomaly detection will draft tests that humans then review, which shifts effort from writing checks to deciding thresholds. The open question is whether quality signals become a first class input to model behaviour, or stay a separate report that nobody reads until something breaks.
